paper.title: Contributions of insula and superior temporal sulcus to interpersonal guilt and responsibility in social decisions

nodes.text: Does being responsible for a risky choice that leaves a partner worse off produce interpersonal guilt — a larger fall in the decision-maker's momentary happiness than when the partner made the same choice?
nodes.description: The behavioural question. Guilt is defined operationally: feeling worse about a partner's bad outcome when you caused it than when they did.
nodes.anchor: The neural mechanisms underlying guilt evoked during such situations of social responsibility are still unknown.

nodes.text: Is the anterior insula, together with its connectivity to prefrontal cortex, the neural substrate of that guilt?
nodes.description: The imaging question about guilt itself: which region responds when the participant is responsible for the partner's low outcome, and how it talks to prefrontal cortex.
nodes.anchor: Next we sought to uncover the neural mechanisms associated with our guilt effect

nodes.text: Does a neural substrate track the participant's responsibility for the partner's outcomes — representing the partner's reward prediction errors more strongly when they follow the participant's own choice?
nodes.description: The imaging question about responsibility rather than guilt: a signal that cares who chose, not whether the outcome was bad.
nodes.anchor: those involved in tracking consequences of participants’ decisions on their partner

nodes.text: Study 1: behavioural experiment, 40 participants, three sessions outside the scanner
nodes.description: Participants chose between safe and risky options for themselves (Solo), for themselves and a partner (Social), or watched the partner choose (Partner), rating happiness every two trials. The partner was another participant.
nodes.anchor: 40 healthy participants (14 male, mean age 26.1, range 22 to 31) participated in Study 1 (behaviour only study)

nodes.text: Study 2: fMRI experiment, 44 participants, two sessions in the scanner
nodes.description: The same task inside a 3T scanner, with longer and variable intervals between events; the partner was an experimenter. All brain results come from this study.
nodes.anchor: 44 healthy participants (19 male, mean (SD) age = 30.6 (6.5), range 23 to 50) participated in Study 2 (fMRI study)

nodes.text: Lottery choice task with Solo, Social and Partner conditions
nodes.description: On each trial a safe amount against a lottery with two equiprobable outcomes. Solo: the choice affects only the participant. Social: the participant chooses for both. Partner: the partner chooses for both. In Social and Partner, each player's lottery is drawn independently.
nodes.anchor: participants were presented with pairs of monetary options (a safe and a risky option; the risky option was a lottery with equally probable high and low outcomes)

nodes.text: Partner choices simulated by an expected-value-maximising algorithm
nodes.description: To keep the partner's behaviour identical across participants, the partner's choices were made by an algorithm that always picked the higher expected value. Participants were not told.
nodes.anchor: We contrasted this condition with similar choices made by a simple expected-value-maximizing algorithm posing for the partner

nodes.text: Icebreaker game to create a social bond before the task
nodes.description: Participant and partner met for about fifteen minutes and played a cooperative game, so that the partner's outcomes would matter emotionally.
nodes.anchor: participants were paired with a partner and played an “ice-breaker” game that created a positive social bond between them

nodes.text: Momentary happiness probe every two trials
nodes.description: After every second outcome, participants rated how happy they felt on a continuous scale; the ratings are the dependent measure for the behavioural analyses.
nodes.anchor: Momentary happiness was assessed every two trials in a similar manner to previous studies by Rutledge and colleagues

nodes.text: Risk-attitude estimation: risk premium and CARA expected utility
nodes.description: Two measures of how risk-averse each participant was in each condition: a risk premium from a fitted logistic regression, and a constant-absolute-risk-aversion parameter ρ from expected utility theory.
nodes.anchor: we calculated for each participant a “risk premium”, defined as the difference between the expected value of a lottery and its certainty equivalent

nodes.text: Five computational models of momentary happiness
nodes.description: Basic, Inequality, Guilt-envy, Responsibility and Responsibility Redux: exponentially decaying influences of certain rewards, expected values and reward prediction errors, with the Responsibility models adding the partner's prediction errors split by who chose. Compared by AIC, BIC, R² and likelihood-ratio tests; parameter recovery on synthetic data.
nodes.anchor: we fitted computational models to each participant’s happiness data

nodes.text: Linear mixed models of happiness after lottery outcomes
nodes.description: Happiness after Social and Partner lottery outcomes modelled with the participant's outcome, the partner's outcome, who chose, and their interactions; the guilt effect is the partner-outcome × decision-maker interaction.
nodes.anchor: we analysed happiness values reported after outcomes of lottery choices in the Social and Partner conditions using conventional linear mixed models

nodes.text: fMRI acquisition, GLMs and region-of-interest mixed models
nodes.description: 3T EPI BOLD; a conventional GLM of the trial events (GLM1) and a model-based GLM with the Responsibility model's variables as regressors (GLM2); regions of interest from the lottery-versus-safe outcome contrast analysed with linear mixed models.
nodes.anchor: We analysed the BOLD responses of brain regions engaged during decision-making and at the time of receiving the outcomes of the choice using conventional as well as computational model-based analyses

nodes.text: Seed-to-voxel psychophysiological interaction from left insula and left STS
nodes.description: Whole-brain connectivity during the choice phase from two seeds, looking for a Condition × Choice interaction.
nodes.anchor: we used the left insula and left STS as seed regions for whole-brain seed-to-voxel psychophysiological interaction analyses

nodes.text: Comparison with the published guilt-related brain signature
nodes.description: Each participant's guilt-related activation map was projected onto Yu et al.'s multivariate guilt signature; a positive dot product means resemblance.
nodes.anchor: we compared this brain signature to the neural responses obtained in our task

nodes.text: Rutledge et al. (2016)
nodes.description: Prior work establishing that momentary happiness in a probabilistic reward task is explained by recent rewards, expectations and prediction errors — the modelling framework this paper adopts and extends.
nodes.anchor: Following Rutledge and colleagues’ methodology, which considers that changes in momentary happiness in response to outcomes of a probabilistic reward task are explained by the combined influence of recent reward expectations and prediction errors

nodes.text: Edelson et al. (2018)
nodes.description: A study of seeking or avoiding responsibility for group outcomes, which found responsibility aversion not explained by guilt, and insula–TPJ connectivity varying with it.
nodes.anchor: most participants displayed responsibility aversion, and this effect could not be explained by guilt, suggesting people associate a psychological cost with assuming responsibility for others’ outcomes

nodes.text: Yu et al. (2014)
nodes.description: A guilt paradigm in which participants could bear part of a partner's pain; anterior insula and anterior middle cingulate were more active when the pain followed the participant's own errors.
nodes.anchor: The level of pain taken, indicative of guilt, and activations in anterior middle cingulate cortex and aIns were higher when the pain followed errors made only by the participant rather than by both players

nodes.text: Responsibility for a social choice that yields a low outcome for a partner produces interpersonal guilt, felt as a larger decrease in momentary happiness than when the partner made the same choice.
nodes.description: The paper's central bet: it is being responsible for the partner's bad outcome, not the bad outcome itself, that hurts.
nodes.anchor: choosing a risky option in such a case may evoke guilt when the outcome for others is negative

nodes.text: The anterior insula is the neural substrate of that guilt, responding more when the participant is responsible for a low outcome affecting the partner.
nodes.description: The insula has been linked to guilt in earlier work; the bet is that it carries the guilt effect here.
nodes.anchor: Given the documented association between anterior insula and guilt (see Introduction)

nodes.text: Connectivity between the guilt- and responsibility-related regions and prefrontal cortex changes with who decides and with the type of choice.
nodes.description: A bet about how the insula and STS talk to prefrontal cortex during choice, depending on whether the choice is risky and whether it affects the partner.
nodes.anchor: We hypothesized that connectivity with regions that showed guilt- and responsibility-related responses during the outcome phase (see previous paragraph) might change depending on whether participants made decisions for themselves only or for themselves and their partner

nodes.text: A neural substrate tracks the participant's responsibility for the partner's outcomes, representing the partner's reward prediction errors more strongly when they arise from the participant's own choice.
nodes.description: A bet about responsibility rather than guilt: some region should care who caused the partner's surprise, good or bad.
nodes.anchor: search for networks sensitive to reward prediction errors resulting from participant or partner choices

nodes.text: Happiness fell more after a partner's low outcome when the participant rather than the partner had chosen the lottery.
nodes.description: The guilt effect, in both studies: the same bad outcome for the partner hurts more when you caused it. Figure 3D and 3H. The authors read it as 'simple guilt'.
nodes.anchor: When the partner received the low lottery outcome, participant happiness was lower when they rather than the partner had chosen the lottery

nodes.text: A happiness model that weights the partner's reward prediction errors from the participant's own choices separately fits best, and those weights are above zero.
nodes.description: Of five computational models, the Responsibility model wins the likelihood-ratio tests in both studies, and the term for the partner's surprises caused by the participant is reliably positive. Table 1, Figure 3C and 3G.
nodes.anchor: the Responsibility model fitted better than all the other models, including the Responsibility Redux model

nodes.text: The participant's own reward prediction errors influenced happiness more than the partner's.
nodes.description: Responsibility matters, but one's own surprises matter more.
nodes.anchor: Participants’ reward prediction errors (sRPE) influenced happiness more than partner’s reward prediction errors

nodes.text: Momentary happiness tracked the rewards both the participant and the partner received on the current trial.
nodes.description: The basic premise of the modelling, replicated here: happiness follows recent rewards, one's own and the partner's. Figure 3A, 3B, 3E, 3F.
nodes.anchor: participant momentary happiness correlated with rewards obtained in the current trial by the participant and by the partner

nodes.text: Being the decision-maker lowered happiness, independent of the outcome.
nodes.description: A separate finding, not the guilt effect: deciding for others costs something even when nothing bad happens. The authors read it as the 'weight of responsibility', as in Edelson et al.
nodes.anchor: found happiness to be lower when the participant chose, independent of the outcome

nodes.text: Responsibility did not change happiness after good outcomes for the partner.
nodes.description: The guilt effect is specific to bad outcomes, as guilt predicts.
nodes.anchor: Responsibility for choices did not influence happiness following positive lottery outcomes for the partner

nodes.text: Risk preferences were very similar whether deciding for oneself alone or for oneself and the partner, with only a weak tendency to more caution in the Social condition in Study 1.
nodes.description: Risk premiums did not differ in either study; the ρ parameter was slightly higher in Social in Study 1 only. Figure 2. The authors conclude they have no strong evidence of a difference.
nodes.anchor: participants showed very similar risk preferences when making decisions affecting only themselves (Solo condition) or themselves and their partner (Social condition)

nodes.text: Insula activity was higher for the partner's low outcomes when the participant rather than the partner had chosen.
nodes.description: The guilt effect in the brain: insula regions of interest mirrored the behavioural interaction, and a voxel-wise analysis found a small left anterior insula cluster doing the same. Figure 4E and 4F.
nodes.anchor: activation in our insula ROIs increased in situations during which participants experienced guilt for low outcomes impacting their partner

nodes.text: Connectivity between the left anterior insula and the right inferior frontal gyrus varied with condition and choice, highest for risky choices for oneself and safe choices for both.
nodes.description: How the insula talks to prefrontal cortex depends on what is chosen and for whom. Figure 5. The authors suggest the right IFG is sensitive to guilt-related information.
nodes.anchor: a cluster in the right inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) whose connectivity to the insula (the seed region) was highest when participants made Risky choices for themselves and Safe choices for both players

nodes.text: Connectivity between the left STS and left inferior frontal gyrus showed the opposite pattern, but did not survive correction.
nodes.description: A weak, uncorrected result the authors call anecdotal, read as information from STS being relayed to IFG. Supplementary Figure 2.
nodes.anchor: connectivity with the left STS (the seed region) showed the opposite pattern

nodes.text: A left superior temporal sulcus cluster responded more to the partner's reward prediction errors when they followed the participant's own choice than the partner's.
nodes.description: The responsibility signal: a region that tracks the partner's surprises more when the participant caused them. Figure 4H and 4I. The authors read it as monitoring the consequences of one's decisions on others.
nodes.anchor: We found this effect in one cluster within the left STS

nodes.text: Choosing for both oneself and the partner, rather than for oneself alone, engaged the precuneus, left temporo-parietal junction and medial prefrontal cortex.
nodes.description: The social-decision network, replicating earlier work; precuneus and TPJ were most active for risky choices in the Social condition. Figure 4B and 4C.
nodes.anchor: Three significant clusters of voxels were identified (Figure 4B and Supplementary Table 3), in the precuneus

nodes.text: Receiving lottery outcomes, compared with safe outcomes, engaged bilateral anterior insula, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, right STS, ventral striatum, right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and inferior parietal lobe.
nodes.description: The regions sensitive to risky outcomes, which define the regions of interest for the guilt analyses. Figure 4D.
nodes.anchor: Cluster of voxels more active during receipt of lottery outcomes than outcomes of safe choices were identified in the bilateral anterior insula

nodes.text: The guilt-related activation patterns resembled the published guilt-related brain signature.
nodes.description: Convergent evidence that what the insula analysis found is guilt: individual maps projected positively onto Yu et al.'s signature, though the match did not track individual differences in the behavioural effect.
nodes.anchor: The “neurometrics” analysis of our guilt-related activation maps showed a significant similarity to a published guilt-related brain signature

nodes.text: The larger drop in happiness after the partner's low outcome is disappointment at the participant's own outcome, not guilt about the partner's.
nodes.description: Rival to the guilt reading. Argued against: the effect holds whether the participant's own lottery came out high or low.
nodes.anchor: The “guilt effect” occurred whether the participant received the high lottery outcome

nodes.text: Being responsible simply amplifies the participant's reaction to all of the partner's outcomes, good or bad.
nodes.description: Rival to the guilt reading. Argued against: responsibility made no difference after good partner outcomes.
nodes.anchor: Responsibility for choices did not influence happiness following positive lottery outcomes for the partner

nodes.text: Choosing for two people changes how much risk participants take, so the differences between conditions reflect different choices rather than guilt.
nodes.description: Rival, handled by checking risk attitudes directly. Risk premiums did not differ; a slight shift in ρ in Study 1 gives it weak support. The authors conclude they have no strong evidence of a difference.
nodes.anchor: To better assess whether people’s risk preferences varied between the Solo and the Social condition

nodes.text: Happiness tracks the inequality between the participant's and the partner's rewards; responsibility for the partner's surprises adds nothing.
nodes.description: Rival account built into the model comparison as the Inequality and Guilt-envy models. Argued against: the Responsibility model beat both in both studies.
nodes.anchor: we assessed the fit of an ‘Inequality’ model that included one term modelling the difference between the participant and partner outcomes

nodes.text: What participants felt was empathy for the partner, a sense of failure or bad luck, or some emotion other than guilt.
nodes.description: Raised by the authors themselves, since no one was asked what they felt. Left open on the behavioural measure ('we cannot exclude'), then argued against on the neural one: the activation maps resembled a published guilt signature, 'we thus believe that our participants did experience guilt'.
nodes.anchor: we cannot exclude the possibility that they have instead or in addition felt empathy for their partner, a feeling of failure or bad luck, or some other emotion

nodes.text: Because the partner's choices were really an algorithm, participants were emotionally detached from the partner's outcomes and the effects do not reflect a social interaction.
nodes.description: A limitation the authors raise and answer: partner outcomes did move participants' happiness, so they were not detached.
